rv.q: The best musical based on American history since 'Hamilton'.
Taub's show is a triumph, with an enthralling plot, moving emotional moments and exceptional music and lyricism.
It is just a really, really good musical. Comparisons to Hamilton are obvious and I think justified in all the best ways.
Stirring and powerful, the production feels eerily current because of today's political discussions around voting and Taub's sharp framing of a story that has driving music and anthemic lyrics.
Every member of the all-female cast of 17, meanwhile, delivers a knockout-caliber performance that sells both the message and the dimension of their portrayals.
The all-female cast is top-to-bottom outstanding, with pure intensity from Keleher and sly regality Ramirez especially.
"Suffs" is glorious and exhilarating and makes you want to learn more about the women's suffragist movement.
Despite being written only a few years back, the show is in many ways a good, old-fashioned musical. It follows a tried and true structure and utilizes common platitudes of musical theater.
The company is solid from top to bottom, the women really starting to impress with the aforementioned crowd-pleaser, "G. A. B."
Its message feels less like a history lesson, and more like a call to action.
At times, that means dense lyrics that almost feel unwieldy, which Taub cleverly addresses early on.
Among the smartest parts of 'Suffs' is that there's no final dreams-come-true moment.
Suffs is a very ambitious history lesson with so many characters that we don't really get to know any of them well — so we care about the issue but not the individual people.
"Suffs" feels somewhat incomplete. The musical acknowledges racial tensions within the movement, but its treatment of Black characters and their experience is cursory and underdeveloped.
There's a tension within 'Suffs' that isn't fully grappled with: How do you reconcile the gains of an inspiring, important feminist victory with the reality of its shortcomings?
The Black suffragists who appear in "Suffs" serve as plot devices more often than not.
In Suffs, good, clear, illuminating rage is nowhere in evidence.
